clue.text: The cab toll isn't fixed, but rather, spread.

indicators.note: letters that are not fixed in place are free to be rearranged

parts.note: the ten letters of these three words are the fodder

explanation.surface: A grumble that taxi fares are not set but vary widely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'isn't fixed' tells you to rearrange THE CAB TOLL. 'Spread' looks like part of the fare complaint, but it is the definition, in its sense of a cloth laid over a table.
explanation.definitionFit: A spread is a cover laid over furniture, and a cloth covering a dining table is one such covering.

clue.text: Hamlet evidently didn't imply it was too high.

definitions.text: Hamlet evidently didn't imply it was too high

parts.words: Hamlet evidently didn't imply it was too high
parts.note: in 'To be or not to be' Hamlet weighs whether life is worth its pains and chooses to go on, so for him the price of staying alive was not excessive

explanation.walkthrough: 'Too high' sounds like a complaint about prices; the joke is that Hamlet's soliloquy weighs the price of being alive at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The economic phrase for what everyday necessities cost is punned on as the price of staying alive, which Hamlet judged bearable.

clue.text: The air of an old sailor suggests one should waft a little thistle in someone's directoon.

definitions.text: The air of an old sailor
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a traditional sea shanty

definitions.text: one should waft a little thistle in someone's directoon
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read literally: puff the fluff of a thistle towards a fellow

explanation.walkthrough: 'Air' means a tune here. Read word by word, the shanty's title is an instruction to send thistledown towards a man.
explanation.definitionFit: The title is that of a well-known sea shanty, and read literally it tells you to puff fluffy seed towards a fellow.

clue.text: It means he goes out.

parts.note: the Latin word is the third person singular of exire, literally 'he goes out', used as a stage direction

explanation.walkthrough: The Latin stage direction translates as 'he leaves', which is how the English word for a way out came about.
explanation.definitionFit: In play scripts the Latin verb tells an actor to leave the stage, literally saying that he departs.

clue.text: Shelters, perhaps, from so long a composition.

indicators.note: a composition puts things together in a new arrangement, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the seven letters of these three words are the fodder

explanation.surface: Taking cover from a piece of writing or music that goes on too long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composition' rearranges SO LONG A. 'Shelters, perhaps' reads as a verb, but it is a noun: the 'perhaps' marks these as examples of sheltered waters.
explanation.definitionFit: Shallow bodies of water cut off by reefs or sandbars are calm havens, an example of a sheltered place.

clue.text: Funny he was in ancient Rome!

definitions.text: Funny he was in ancient Rome!

parts.words: Funny he was in ancient Rome!
parts.note: the Roman playwright Publius Terentius Afer wrote comedies

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation sounds like surprise that someone was in Rome; it is a description of a Roman writer of comedies.
explanation.definitionFit: This Roman dramatist of the second century BC wrote six surviving comedies, so he was a comic writer of ancient Rome.

clue.text: Shut out in this manner?

indicators.note: out describes the word shut being put out of its order, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: the four letters of this word are the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether this is how a person gets excluded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shut out' reads as one phrase meaning excluded; split it, and 'out' works on 'Shut' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means in the way described, a direct synonym for this manner of doing something.

clue.text: It might be found near the lift.

indicators.note: says the answer could be found by reworking the next words, so their letters are reordered

parts.note: the seven letters of these two words are the fodder

explanation.surface: A guess at where something is kept: close to the elevator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'near the lift' reads as a location, but 'might be found' rearranges NEAR THE and 'lift' is the definition, in its sense of raise someone's spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone heart or encouragement is to raise their spirits, the verb sense of lift.

clue.text: In the navy, would one get only a sandwich and a glass of water, perhaps?

definitions.text: In the navy, would one get only a sandwich and a glass of water, perhaps?

parts.words: In the navy, would one get only a sandwich and a glass of water, perhaps?
parts.note: a submarine is a long sandwich in American usage, and a chaser is a drink taken after spirits, here water

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sub' or submarine is the long bread roll; a chaser is a drink downed after another. Together they name a warship that hunts submarines.
explanation.definitionFit: A small naval vessel designed to hunt and attack enemy undersea boats, punned on as a sandwich followed by a drink.

clue.text: The character of the Assyrians, Babylonians, etc.

definitions.text: The character of the Assyrians, Babylonians, etc.

parts.words: The character of the Assyrians, Babylonians, etc.
parts.note: character here means a form of writing, not personality

explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests national temperament; it means a script, the wedge-shaped writing pressed into clay tablets.
explanation.definitionFit: The wedge-shaped script of Mesopotamia was used by Sumerians, Babylonians and Assyrians for their written records.

clue.text: Wearing, for example, around a sculptor.

indicators.note: around says the letters for 'for example' go on either side of the sculptor's name

parts.note: EG is the abbreviation of exempli gratia, for example
Auguste Rodin, the French sculptor of The Thinker

explanation.surface: Someone wearing a garment near a sculptor, as if dressing for a studio visit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' wraps the abbreviation round the sculptor, Rodin of The Thinker. 'Wearing' suggests clothing, but here it is the participle of wear away.
explanation.definitionFit: Wearing in the sense of gradually abrading or using up matches the participle for slowly washing or grinding something away.

clue.text: Evidently some disturbance in the plant.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a noisy row or commotion
second meaning: the garden plant with edible pink stalks

explanation.walkthrough: 'Evidently' is padding that makes the surface read as gardening trouble; the word means both a row and the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is American slang for a heated argument, especially on the baseball field, and is also the vegetable grown for its stalks.

clue.text: Only productive when made by sacrifice.

definitions.text: Only productive when made by sacrifice

parts.words: Only productive when made by sacrifice
parts.note: in baseball, a batter normally gains nothing by being retired, except with a sacrifice bunt or fly that advances a runner

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sacrifice' suggests a moral or religious act; in baseball a sacrifice is a play where the batter deliberately gets put out so a runner can advance or score.
explanation.definitionFit: Retiring a batter usually helps only the fielding side, so these retirements help the batting team solely in sacrifice plays.

clue.text: Flower pots tie in a better arrangement, possibly.

indicators.note: putting the letters into a better arrangement means reordering them

parts.note: the ten letters of these four words are the fodder

explanation.surface: Advice to a florist that some flower pots might be tied together more neatly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'better arrangement, possibly' rearranges POTS TIE IN A; the surface is about flower pots, but 'Flower' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This Mexican shrub with red bracts is sold as a Christmas plant, an example of a bloom.

clue.text: Could it describe an agreement to have a bill contain a rate that isn't fixed?

indicators.note: the word bill is told to hold the next letters within it

parts.note: the four letters of this word are used as written

indicators.note: a rate that is not fixed is free to have its letters shuffled

explanation.surface: A question about a contract under which an invoice carries a floating interest rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that isn't fixed' shuffles the two words 'a rate' into ATERA, and 'contain' sets that inside 'bill', which looks like an invoice but only lends its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An agreement made between two parties or nations is described by this adjective meaning two-sided.

clue.text: Sort of this to a sort of 13, worn by some men.

indicators.note: a sort of something here means its letters rearranged, so this answer plus the next two words, mixed up, give the other entry

parts.note: the answer to 13 across, the Christmas flower
these letters are added to the answer before the mixing

explanation.surface: A cryptic cross-reference: a kind of accessory that some men wear, linked to the flower answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of this to a' means an anagram of this answer plus TOA, which must equal 'a sort of 13', an anagram of POINSETTIA; take T, O and A out of POINSETTIA and PINSETI remains.
explanation.definitionFit: These are decorative clips or pins that fasten a necktie to the shirt, an accessory chiefly worn by men.

clue.text: Master of Turkey.

parts.note: an Ottoman title of respect for a man of education or standing, like 'sir'

explanation.walkthrough: The phrasing suggests a ruler of the country, such as a sultan, but the word is the polite Turkish title for a gentleman.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ottoman honorific was given to officials and learned men, much like calling someone master or sir.

clue.text: With this, you should be lucky to be well-known.

definitions.text: With this, you should be lucky to be well-known

parts.words: With this, you should be lucky to be well-known
parts.note: the phrase pairs renown with riches; the clue matches 'lucky' to the second noun and 'well-known' to the first

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as advice, but it describes the two nouns of the phrase: one makes you well-known, the other is luck.
explanation.definitionFit: Celebrity and wealth or good luck together form the stock phrase for success, and luck is one sense of the second noun.

clue.text: See 2
Allow to get into deep trouble when empty.

indicators.note: to trouble something is to stir it up, so the combined letters are mixed

parts.note: to let is to allow
the four letters of this word are used as written

explanation.surface: Letting someone fall into serious difficulty once the cupboard is bare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get into' just joins LET to DEEP, giving the pool DEEPLET, and 'trouble' rearranges all seven letters. 'Deep trouble' looks like a fixed phrase, but 'trouble' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhaust or use up a supply is to drain it, which is the verb sense of empty.

clue.text: See 17
Shakespeare's lover sighed like one.

parts.note: in the 'seven ages of man' speech in As You Like It

explanation.walkthrough: Jaques's 'All the world's a stage' speech describes the lover sighing like this, a hot roaring oven.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare compared the lover's heavy breathing to the roaring draught of a large oven or kiln.

clue.text: Straighten out.

parts.note: the phrase is read literally, to take the kinks or coils out of something

explanation.walkthrough: 'Straighten out' suggests sorting a problem; read literally it means removing turns from a rope or wire.
explanation.definitionFit: To undo the coils or kinks of something wound up leaves it straight, the literal sense of the phrasal verb.

clue.text: Republicans not about to be hosts, perhaps.

definitions.text: Republicans not about to be hosts, perhaps

parts.words: Republicans not about to be hosts, perhaps
parts.note: take RE (about) from the front of Republicans and you have publicans, pub keepers, who are the hosts the answer names

explanation.walkthrough: 'Republicans' sounds political, but without RE, a crossword word for about, it becomes publicans, and publicans are people who run inns; the answer is their other name rather than the letters themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: Landlords who run inns or pubs receive guests and serve them, so they are hosts by trade.

clue.text: Septennial problem?

parts.note: septennial means occurring every seven years; the clue points to the idiom about restlessness seven years into a marriage

explanation.walkthrough: 'Septennial' sounds like a dry calendar term; it points to the seven-year itch, also a Marilyn Monroe film.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a restless urge said to strike couples about seven years into marriage, a recurring trouble every seven years.

clue.text: Othello was one to bring up some space.

indicators.note: in a down clue, bringing something up reads its letters from the bottom

parts.note: room means space

explanation.surface: Othello, the soldier, making a little space for himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to bring up' reads ROOM upwards, as this is a down clue. Othello is Shakespeare's 'Moor of Venice', a North African.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's tragic general is a North African of the people historically called Moors.

clue.text: It started around 1000 BC, that is, about a misplaced organ…

indicators.note: about says the letters for 'that is' go round the rest

parts.note: IE is the abbreviation of id est, that is

indicators.note: an organ whose parts are misplaced has its letters out of order

parts.note: the five letters of this word are rearranged

explanation.surface: A history lesson about something beginning three thousand years ago, then a stray organ.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misplaced' mixes up 'organ' into RONAG and 'about' wraps id est's abbreviation round it. 'Around' in the definition is the date's approximation, not an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaeological period when iron tools replaced bronze began in many regions roughly a millennium before Christ.

clue.text: …but then, no age is bad for such feelings!

indicators.note: letters gone bad are spoiled out of their proper order

parts.note: these letters are part of the fodder
these letters complete the fodder

explanation.surface: Following on from the previous clue: at no time of life are such sufferings unpleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad' rearranges NO AGE IS. The ellipsis links back to the misplaced organ, as though the pain followed it; the clue stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer means intense physical or mental pains, the kind of feelings the surface pictures.

clue.text: Go with Burns in full complement.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: in Robert Burns's Scots, the verb for to go
second meaning: a whole crew or team of workers

explanation.walkthrough: Robert Burns was the Scottish poet who wrote in Scots dialect, where this word means go; it also means a full crew.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots the verb means to walk or go, and as a noun it is a body of workers forming a complete team.

clue.text: Perhaps one on the 4th of July.

definitions.text: Perhaps one on the 4th of July

parts.words: Perhaps one on the 4th of July
parts.note: Independence Day in the US is a day of parties and fireworks

explanation.walkthrough: The 4th of July is American Independence Day, and anyone marking it with parades or fireworks fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who marks a festive occasion with festivities is a reveller, and the national holiday is a typical occasion.
